passage:
"Dhruv, read this before I send it." Yogesh turned the laptop around on the dining table.
Dhruv read aloud. "'Third late login this month. Consider this your final warning. Excuses will not be entertained.' Who's it for?"
"Salma, on my team. She's always ten minutes late."
"Why?"
"No idea. Didn't ask."
"Would you talk to Ammi like this if she was late?"
Yogesh laughed, then didn't. "No. I'd ask if the bus broke down."
"So?"
Yogesh deleted the message. "I've become that supervisor, haven't I? The one we used to complain about."
"A bit."
"Okay. Tomorrow I ask her what's going on, first. And I'll ask my manager to look at how we handle lates, so it's not just my mood."
"And ask the team?"
"Anonymous form. 'What one thing do I do that makes work worse?'" Yogesh groaned. "That'll be fun."
"Fun for me," Dhruv grinned.

qa.q: What did Yogesh's draft message call it?
qa.a: A 'final warning' for a third late login this month.

qa.q: What does Yogesh's laugh that suddenly stops suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Yogesh suddenly sees the message is harsher than anything Yogesh would say at home, and feels uncomfortable at becoming the supervisor they used to complain about.

qa.q: Which choices did Yogesh make after deleting the message?
qa.a: To ask Salma what's going on first, to ask the manager to review how lates are handled, and to send the team an anonymous form.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt if she had received the first message?
qa.a: Salma would likely feel judged without being heard, since nobody had asked why she was late.

grounding: At home, a young supervisor asks whether they would treat family this way, then seeks a manager's review and honest team input.

passage: This is Jasleen, writing it down so I don't forget. Three months into supervising the packing floor at the warehouse, I caught myself timing Rajni's washroom breaks on the clipboard. Rajni is fifty and has two grandchildren. At a family wedding I'd give her my chair. Standing there with the clipboard, I asked myself: would I do this to my own Bua? The answer was so obviously no that I felt sick. That week I did three things. I wrote the break rules on the notice board, so nobody depended on my mood. I asked our HR head to sit in on one shift a month and tell me what they saw. And I left a box by the water cooler: 'What should I stop doing?' The first note said, 'Stop the clipboard.' I did.

qa.q: What was Jasleen timing on the clipboard?
qa.a: Rajni's washroom breaks.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen feel sick standing with the clipboard?
qa.a: Asking 'would I do this to my own Bua?' made the answer obviously no, and Jasleen was shaken by the gap between the work self and the real self.

qa.q: Which of Jasleen's three steps adds a check from outside, and why does that choice matter?
qa.a: Asking the HR head to sit in on one shift a month; someone outside the role can spot drift that Jasleen might miss.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel when the clipboard stops?
qa.a: Rajni would likely feel trusted and respected again, no longer watched like a suspect 🙂

grounding: A young supervisor asks whether they'd treat a worker this way outside work, then adds clear rules, oversight and honest feedback.

passage:
Ops head's note, Monday. Baljeet.
Lokesh has been shift supervisor on the bottling line for four months. I've watched him closely, since new supervisors here often turn sharp by month three. Last week I saw him start to shout at Kiran over a jammed conveyor, then stop mid-sentence. Afterwards he came to my cabin. 'Sir, I was about to talk to her the way I'd never talk to anyone outside this gate. Can you sit in on my Friday huddles for a while?' He also asked to put the line targets and his own performance notes on the board, so the team sees what he is judged on. At the huddle he asked, 'What am I doing that makes your day harder?' Two people answered.
What I did next: I agreed to join Fridays and suggested the other supervisors try the same practice.

qa.q: What was Lokesh about to shout at Kiran over?
qa.a: A jammed conveyor.

qa.q: What does Lokesh stopping mid-sentence suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: It suggests Lokesh felt alarmed on noticing he was about to treat Kiran in a way he never would outside the gate, and caught the role taking over.

qa.q: Which of Lokesh's requests made his work more open to checks?
qa.a: Asking Baljeet to sit in on Friday huddles, and putting the line targets and his own performance notes on the board for the team to see.

qa.q: How might Kiran see a supervisor who stops mid-shout?
qa.a: Kiran might feel relieved and more willing to speak honestly at huddles, seeing a supervisor who checks himself.

grounding: An ops head records a young supervisor catching himself, inviting oversight, sharing targets openly and asking the team for input.

passage:
Tuesday, after shift

Three months as housekeeping supervisor at the hotel. Today I caught myself. Zubin had missed a corner under a bed in 412, and I was standing over him with the checklist, saying, "How many times do I have to tell you people?" He's twenty-two, sends half his pay home, and always holds the lift for guests.

I stopped mid-sentence and asked myself: would I talk to Zubin like this at the bus stop? No. Never.

So what's happening to me in that uniform?

Three things I did today:
1. Wrote the room-check rules on the staff board, so it's the rule, not my mood.
2. Asked the front-office manager to walk my floors with me once a week and tell me honestly what she sees.
3. At the evening huddle I said, "Tell me one thing I do that makes your work harder." Silence. Then Zubin said, "Standing over us, ma'am." Fair.

- Ritu

qa.q: Which room had Zubin missed a corner in?
qa.a: He missed a corner under a bed in room 412.

qa.q: What made Ritu stop mid-sentence?
qa.a: She suddenly asked herself whether she would speak to Zubin like that at the bus stop and knew she would never, which showed her the role was changing her.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's three steps protects most against the role taking over, and why?
qa.a: Writing the rules on the board and asking the front-office manager to walk her floors make things transparent and checked, so her mood no longer decides.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt saying 'Standing over us' at the huddle?
qa.a: He was probably nervous but relieved to be asked, and it may have made him trust his supervisor more.

grounding: A young supervisor asks whether she would treat a worker this way outside work, then adds clear rules, outside oversight and a request for honest input.

passage:
Rekha: Charu, need to tell someone. I snapped at a resident today
Charu: at the hostel? what happened
Rekha: a girl came back 10 min after curfew. I made her wait outside the gate while I lectured her
Rekha: in the rain
Charu: oh Rekha
Rekha: I know. two months as warden and I'm turning into the warden we hated
Charu: what made you notice
Rekha: she said "sorry ma'am" like I was a jail guard. I thought, would I leave my own cousin outside in the rain? never
Charu: so what now
Rekha: apologised to her tonight. then wrote the late-return rules on the notice board so it's not about my mood
Rekha: asked the trust secretary to check the late register with me every month
Rekha: and I'm putting a suggestion box by the office. "what should the warden stop doing"
Charu: that's brave
Rekha: or scary. we'll see

qa.q: How late was the girl who came back after curfew?
qa.a: She came back ten minutes after curfew.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she heard the girl say 'sorry ma'am'?
qa.a: She felt shocked and ashamed, because she was being treated like a jail guard and realised she would never leave her own cousin outside in the rain.

qa.q: Which of Rekha's steps keeps the warden role in check, and why?
qa.a: Posting the rules, asking the trust secretary to review the late register monthly, and a suggestion box add transparency, oversight and honest input.

qa.q: How might the residents see the suggestion box by the office?
qa.a: They might be surprised at first but feel safer and more respected, knowing the warden wants to hear what should change.

grounding: A young warden pauses to ask whether she would treat someone this way outside work, apologises and sets up clear rules, oversight and honest input.
